title: Timing 150 minutes: about two minutes a mark
blurb: Pace 70 marks in 150 minutes, decide when a lookup is worth it, and finish with every answer marked.
question: You are on question 30 after 75 minutes, with a matching set and a long processes section still to come. Are you on track, and what do you change?

teach.body: The Practitioner paper gives you 150 minutes for 70 marks: about 2 minutes 9 seconds a mark. With 25% extra time (188 minutes) it is about 2 minutes 41 seconds. There is no negative marking, so a blank scores the same as a wrong answer: every question, and every row of every matching set, should have an answer before time runs out.
teach.cite: PeopleCert PRINCE2 7 Practitioner syllabus, Exam Overview

teach.h: A suggested plan at 2 minutes a mark
teach.caption: Our suggested plan, not a PeopleCert rule. Spending 2 minutes a mark leaves about 10 minutes to review.

head: After question
Standard time
Extra time (2.5 min a mark)
teach.caption: If you are behind at a checkpoint, cut lookups first, not reading of the stems.

teach.h: When to open the book, and when not
teach.body: A lookup is worth it when one fact separates your last two options and that fact sits in a table: a RACI row, a product's headings, an activity's recommended actions. Give it about a minute. Do not look up principles or judgement calls you already understand; reading around a topic burns time without settling the answer. If the lookup fails, choose your best option, flag it and move on.

children.label: Choose the fitting reason, move on
Look it up, about a minute

teach.h: Worked scenario: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre
teach.body: At 101 minutes a candidate reaches a controlling a stage question on Tarnside College (scenario S2). Project manager Leah Whitfield produces highlight reports at the frequency set in the communication management approach, consulting the team manager and project assurance. Is this an appropriate use of 'report highlights'? The candidate is fairly sure it is, but checks the RACI table in chapter 16: the PM is responsible, with the team manager, support and assurance consulted. Verdict confirmed in about 90 seconds: yes.

items: Treat each set as three separate one-mark decisions.
Answer the rows you are sure of first.
Reuse an option freely: options can fit more than one row, or none.
Cap a set at about 6 minutes; guess any stubborn row and flag it.

teach.text: Controlling a stage questions often hinge on which process does what. Reporting highlights, capturing issues and taking corrective action happen in controlling a stage; an exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary, and only after the board has received an exception report and asked for one.

teach.h: Two passes and a final sweep

items: About 2 minutes a mark leaves 10 minutes to review (2.5 with extra time).
Check the clock after questions 13, 31, 49 and 70.
Look up table facts for about a minute; answer judgement from understanding.
Matching sets: three separate marks, options reusable, cap at about 6 minutes.
No negative marking: never leave a question or a matching row blank.

summary: You can now pace the 150-minute paper section by section, decide when a lookup pays, handle matching sets efficiently and finish with every mark attempted. You can also judge controlling a stage activities on the S2 scenario quickly and accurately.

A.q: A candidate sitting the Practitioner paper in standard time finishes question 49, the last practice question, after 115 minutes. Twenty-one process questions and the review remain. How should she handle the processes section?
options: Aim for about 1.5 minutes a question, flagging hard ones
Keep to about 2 minutes 9 seconds a question as planned
Skip the process questions, as they are worth fewer marks
Leave hard ones blank, as wrong answers lose a mark each
A.why: 35 minutes remain for 21 marks, at most about 1 minute 40 seconds each; aiming for about 1.5 minutes a question leaves a few minutes for flagged items. There is no negative marking.

whyNot.1: 21 questions at that pace would need about 45 minutes, more than the 35 left.
whyNot.2: Every question is worth one mark; skipping a section throws away up to 21 marks.
whyNot.3: There is no negative marking, so a blank can only lose marks.

A.q: Tarnside College is in the structural works stage of its Engineering Skills Centre. The project manager learns that the contractor's site team agreed an extra roof light with the lead welding instructor on site, without checking the budget. She captures it as a request for change in the issue register and assesses it before deciding what to do. Is this an appropriate application of 'capture issues and risks', and why?
options: Yes, because each issue is registered and assessed before deciding
Yes, because the senior user controls changes to the requirements
No, because a request for change should go straight to the board
No, because changes agreed on site belong to the delivery process
A.why: In 'capture issues and risks' each issue is registered and then assessed before a course of action is decided (16.4.5).

whyNot.1: True that the senior user controls change to requirements, but this does not explain the PM capturing and assessing the issue.
whyNot.2: Requests for change are captured and assessed first; they go to the change authority or board as the issue management approach sets out.
whyNot.3: Issues raised by the team are captured and assessed by the project manager in controlling a stage.

A.q: During Tarnside's fit-out stage, a one-week slip on the electrical works is forecast. It is within stage tolerance, and the project manager moves fit-out crews between work packages to recover the time. Which role should be accountable for 'take corrective action'?
options: The project manager
The executive
The senior supplier
The team manager
A.why: In the recommended RACI for 'take corrective action', the executive is accountable; the project manager carries out the action and project support is informed (16.4.6).

whyNot.0: The project manager carries out the corrective action but is not accountable for it.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier commits supplier resources; this activity's accountability sits with the executive.
whyNot.3: The team manager delivers the amended work packages; accountability sits with the executive.

B.q: In a matching set on the Tarnside scenario, a candidate is confident that heading C fits the first statement, and thinks heading C also fits the second. What should she do?
options: Choose heading C for the second statement too
Choose a different heading for the second one
Leave the second statement blank to be safe
Pick a heading not yet used by any statement
B.why: Matching options can be used once, more than once or not at all, so repeating C is fine if it fits.

whyNot.1: Options are not limited to one use in a matching set.
whyNot.2: There is no negative marking; a blank cannot score.
whyNot.3: Spreading options evenly is not a rule; each row is matched on its own merits.

B.q: Tarnside's project manager forecasts that the asbestos removal and structural works stage will finish three weeks late, beyond its two-week time tolerance. She starts writing an exception plan in controlling a stage before telling the board. Is this an appropriate application of the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
options: Yes, because an exception plan replaces the current stage plan
Yes, because the PM should forecast and act as early as possible
No, because the board first receives an exception report and decides
No, because exception plans are prepared by the contractor's team manager
B.why: In 'escalate issues and risks' the PM raises an exception report; the board decides, and if it requests an exception plan, the PM prepares it in managing a stage boundary (16.4.7, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: True that an approved exception plan replaces the stage plan, but it is prepared only when the board asks for it.
whyNot.1: Early action here means an early exception report, not an unrequested exception plan.
whyNot.3: The project manager prepares exception plans, in managing a stage boundary.

B.q: With 30 minutes left and 14 questions to go, a candidate meets a Tarnside question on 'report highlights' and cannot decide whether project assurance or the senior user should be consulted. What is the best approach?
options: Read the whole controlling a stage chapter to be sure
Check the controlling a stage RACI table for a minute
Leave it blank and come back if any time remains
Guess at once, as RACI questions carry fewer marks
B.why: This is a table fact that separates two options, and there is about 2 minutes a question left, so a quick check of table 16.2 is worth it.

whyNot.0: Reading the whole chapter costs far more time than finding one RACI row.
whyNot.2: A blank scores nothing and may be forgotten; answer now and flag if unsure.
whyNot.3: Every classic question is worth one mark, RACI questions included.

C.q: Tarnside's board has agreed a stage cost tolerance of plus or minus 3% and monthly highlight reports. Mid-stage, the project manager forecasts a 5% overspend on the fit-out stage. She decides to include it in her next highlight report, due in three weeks. Is this an appropriate application of the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
options: Yes, because highlight reports follow the frequency the board set
Yes, because the overspend is forecast and has not yet happened
No, because the board must approve any overspend arising within the stage
No, because a forecast stage tolerance breach needs an exception report
C.why: When stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, the PM escalates at once with an exception report in 'escalate issues and risks' (16.4.7).

whyNot.0: True that highlight reports follow the board's frequency, but a forecast breach cannot wait for the next one.
whyNot.1: Exceptions are forecasts; that is exactly when to escalate.
whyNot.2: Within stage tolerance the PM can act without the board; here the issue is that tolerance will be breached.

C.q: Tarnside's project manager writes the work package for the mezzanine floor and emails it to the contractor's team manager, telling the team to start on Monday. There has been no discussion of the work package with the team manager. Is this an appropriate application of 'authorize a work package', and why?
options: Yes, because the PM authorizes work packages in controlling a stage
Yes, because the work package sets scope, cost and time tolerances
No, because the PM should agree the work package with the TM first
No, because a contractor's work is authorized by the senior supplier
C.why: The PM co-creates and reviews the work package with the team manager and confirms acceptance before authorizing work (16.4.1).

whyNot.0: True that the PM authorizes work packages, but this does not explain skipping agreement with the TM.
whyNot.1: True that a work package carries these tolerances, but it does not justify issuing it without discussion.
whyNot.3: Work packages are authorized by the project manager, including for contractors.

C.q: When the contractor reports the welding bays complete, Tarnside's project manager checks that each bay has the approvals defined in its product description before recording it as complete and updating the product register. Is this an appropriate application of 'receive completed work package', and why?
options: Yes, because each product needs the approvals in its description
Yes, because the lead instructor will use the bays once they open
No, because product approval happens at the stage boundary
No, because the team manager updates the product register
C.why: Receiving a completed work package includes ensuring each product has its requisite approval, as defined in its product description, then updating the product register (16.4.3).

whyNot.1: True that users will use the bays, but this does not explain the approval check.
whyNot.2: Products are received and approved in controlling a stage as work packages complete.
whyNot.3: The project manager updates the product register when receiving completed work.

reteach.title: Pace it like a long run
reteach.question: A runner with a 150-minute target splits the course into sections and checks the watch at each marker. How does that translate to the paper?

blocks.body: Runners do not check the watch every step; they check at markers. Do the same: four markers at questions 13, 31, 49 and 70. If you are a few minutes behind at a marker, trim lookups. If you are well ahead, you have earned a longer review. Either way, keep moving: one question is worth one mark, however hard it is.

blocks.text: A wrong answer costs nothing extra. A blank row in a matching set is a mark thrown away.

test.q: A candidate sitting the PRINCE2 7 Practitioner exam in a language that is not her native or working language has been awarded 25% extra time. How long does she have?
options: 165 minutes
175 minutes
188 minutes
180 minutes
test.why: 150 minutes plus 25% is 187.5, given as 188 minutes.

whyNot.1: That is the end of the suggested working time at 2.5 minutes a mark, not the time allowed.

explain.body: At 2 minutes a mark, divide the minutes used by two to see which question you should have reached.

test.q: After 60 minutes of the Practitioner paper, a candidate in standard time has just finished question 20. Using a plan of about 2 minutes a mark, how is she doing?
options: On track; question 20 is about right
Ahead; she should be near question 15
Behind; she should be near question 40
Behind; she should be near question 30
test.why: At 2 minutes a mark, 60 minutes should cover about 30 questions, so she is around 10 questions behind.

whyNot.0: 20 questions should take about 40 minutes, so she is behind.
whyNot.1: Question 15 would be about 30 minutes in; she is behind, not ahead.
whyNot.2: Question 40 would need a minute and a half per question, faster than the plan.

explain.body: RACI rows, product headings and activity names are quick to find and easy to forget. Judgement about a principle is slow to look up and should come from understanding.

test.q: A candidate has decided to allow herself about one quick lookup per section of the paper. In the Tarnside processes section, which question is the best use of it?
options: Whether the board is directing the stage effectively
Which role is consulted in 'report highlights'
Whether the project still has business justification
Whether the governors applied 'manage by stages' well
test.why: A RACI row is a table fact that can be found in seconds in the controlling a stage chapter.

whyNot.0: Judging board effectiveness depends on the situation, not a single table entry.
whyNot.2: Business justification is a judgement from the scenario facts.
whyNot.3: Applying a principle is a judgement best answered from understanding.

test.q: A candidate has 8 minutes left. She has flagged five questions and is not sure she filled in every row of the risk matching set. What should she do first?
options: Re-read the scenario booklet from the start
Change the answers she gave most quickly
Make sure every question and row has an answer
Work on the flagged question that took longest
test.why: With no negative marking, an unanswered row is a certain lost mark; securing a complete answer sheet comes first.

whyNot.0: Re-reading the whole booklet uses the remaining time without gaining marks.
whyNot.1: Quick answers are not more likely to be wrong; changing them without reason risks marks.
whyNot.3: One hard question is worth one mark; a blank row elsewhere is also a mark and quicker to secure.
